meta.title: A Hundred Million Yen
meta.sub: in which a birthday party catches fire
meta.logline: Nana's 25th birthday. Haru sneaks in with a ¥900 book, everyone confesses their worst deed, Ryuji arrives with ¥100,000,000, and the money goes into the fire.

shots.text: Twenty years ago, a poor boy lived across the street from the Hotel Kurosaki. Every night he looked up at the fifty-second floor, where a little girl sat in the window, alone.
I counted her lights. When her light went off, I went to sleep. Twenty years.
A hundred million yen. In cash. Women like to see it. Boards like to see it.
Tonight I stop looking up at her window.
You've changed dresses four times. You never change dresses. You buy a dress and then you're right about it.
Mister Togashi is going to stand up tonight and announce me. Like a new restaurant.
And the cardigan? The candy man? His week ended yesterday. Is he coming?
He's not invited. He's staff. Was staff.
Then why do you keep checking your phone?
He sent me a message at three in the morning. It said, good luck tomorrow, I'm awake. That's all. That's the whole message.
That's a pretty good message, Nana.
It's the best message I've ever got. That's what scares me.
My wedding jacket! Nineteen seventy-nine. A little wide in the shoulders.
I think I could fit Kenta in here with me.
Don't put me in the jacket. I'm the getaway plan.
Why do I need a getaway plan? It's a birthday party.
Because you weren't invited, genius. You were hired, and then the week ended. My cousin works in the hotel kitchen. Back door, nine o'clock.
I wrapped her present. Aya at the bookshop made the bow.
Aya Ishida made you a bow? She once threw a dictionary at a customer.
She was very nice. She only called me ridiculous twice.
Haru. Real question. Do you love her?
Nana asked me to decide by Friday. Today is Friday.
And?
I think love is when you notice someone is tired before they notice it themselves. I noticed on Wednesday. So I think I decided on Wednesday, and I just found out today.
I'm writing that down.
He's writing it down. That means it's good.
Invitations only. You again. The cardigan.
Excuse me, sir! I have information. Your wife's birthday is today, and you forgot.
...Is it the ninth? It's the ninth! Oh no.
Konbini on the corner sells flowers. Go. I'll watch the door.
Kenta, is it really his wife's birthday?
It's somebody's birthday. Go!
Oh. Oh no. Six hundred croquettes. And a cake shaped like a swan. And a fountain of chocolate.
I have to count something ugly. The bins. One bin, two bins. Thank you, bins.
The kitchen staff later agreed that it was the first time anyone had thanked the bins.
Happy birthday, Nana!
Thank you, thank you. Twenty-five. Practically a fossil.
Candy man! He came! I told you he'd come!
Haru? How did you get in? Your week finished yesterday.
Through the kitchen. The chef gave me a croquette. I brought you a present. It's a book of sunsets. It's slightly damaged.
Everyone else brought jewellery. Mika brought a pony. An actual pony. It's in the elevator.
Then the pony and I have both made an effort.
...Thank you. I'll read it at three in the morning.
The pony ate a curtain! Nana, the pony ate a whole curtain!
Charge it to Mika. It's her pony.
It's your pony! It's a present!
Does the pony have a name? Everyone should have a name at a birthday party.
Fine. His name is Mister Togashi Junior. He eats paperwork.
Ladies and gentlemen. Before the cake, the board has an announcement about Nana's future.
Not yet, Mister Togashi. First, a game. My birthday, my rules.
Nana. The board has waited a long time. Mister Gozen is on his way.
The board can wait one more game. It's good for them. Builds character.
Everybody confesses the worst thing they've ever done. Honestly. If you lie, you leave.
Okay, me first. I bought half of my followers. Forty thousand of them are bots in a basement somewhere.
I once deleted a song my best friend wrote, because it was better than mine. He never knew.
When we were fourteen, I told a magazine that Nana's mother left. For money. For a pair of shoes.
I know, Sora. I forgave you at sixteen. They were very good shoes.
...You never said.
You never asked.
I decline to play. Confession is not a business practice.
Then you'll leave, Mister Togashi?
...I once told the board your father called on your birthday. He didn't. He hasn't for nine years.
I know. I always knew. Haru, your turn.
When I was nine, I told Grandma I wasn't scared of the dark anymore, so she wouldn't worry.
But I was. Every night. So I left the lighthouse lamp on all night, and told her it was for the ships. Really it was for me.
That's my worst thing. I lied to my grandmother, for six years, and saved several ships by accident.
That's your worst thing? That's the nicest worst thing I've ever heard.
My worst thing is that I say yes. To everything. I say yes, and then I hate whoever made me say it.
That's not your worst thing, Nana. That's somebody else's worst thing, that happened to you.
...What?
The people who made you say yes. That's their worst thing. You were just very polite about it for twenty-five years.
Oh my god. Is anyone else crying? I'm crying. My lashes are falling off.
Sorry I'm late. I was counting. Happy birthday, Nana.
One hundred million yen. Cash. For you, and the board. Say yes, and it's yours.
And you. The cardigan. How much to walk out that door and never come back?
Usually nine hundred yen, plus a bow. But I'm not for sale today. It's her birthday.
Everyone is for sale.
Then you must be very lonely, Mister Gozen. Buying things is a lonely way to have company.
A very generous proposal. The board approves.
And you, Haru? What's your offer? A hundred yen umbrella?
I don't have an offer. I have a window and a cactus and a library card.
But if you're ever awake at three in the morning, with nobody to call, I'm usually awake too. You can call me. That's all. That's my whole offer.
That's not an offer. That's a phone number.
No. It's the only offer tonight that isn't a price.
Did the cardigan just... propose? With a phone number?
Shut up, Mika. It's the best proposal I've ever heard and I've heard nine.
You want to buy me, Ryuji? Watch your price burn.
Nana! That was a hundred million yen!
Let it burn! I have more. That's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen a woman do.
Nana. You don't have to prove anything. Not to them. Not to me.
That's the problem, Haru. You're the only one here who didn't want to buy me. You'd want to keep me. Gently. Every day.
And I'd ruin you. An idiot deserves better than me.
Car's outside.
Then let's go before I change my mind. Happy birthday to me.
You okay, candy man?
I think so. I think I just haven't fainted yet. It's coming.
For what it's worth, I've known her eleven years. I've never seen her burn anything except a bridge.
Is it still her birthday?
For three more minutes.
She'll come back, man. She always comes back. She's dramatic, not stupid.
I know. I'm not worried about her coming back. I'm worried about her being alone in a car with a man who counted her lights for twenty years.
How do you know that?
He looked at her the way I look at sunsets. Except I let sunsets leave.
Then I'd like to stand by the window for three minutes.
Happy birthday, Nana. I'm awake. Just in case.
My cousin saw them leave. She got in his car. She didn't look back.
I'm sorry, Mister Mishima. I'm not even writing it down.
That's all right. She took the book of sunsets with her. She held it the whole way to the car. Kenta's cousin said so.
He did say that. How did you know?
I didn't. I hoped. Hoping is like knowing, but earlier.
All right. That one I'm writing down.

Next time on Beautiful Idiot: I visit Ryuji, because he looked lonely, and we swap presents. Aya takes me to a festival. Then two very strong women meet in a café, and it doesn't go well. Brothers. I'm bringing Lev for moral support.
